tagline: Hairpin curves link Lake Tahoe, a high pass and Reno’s edge
intro: Mount Rose Highway climbs the Carson Range from Lake Tahoe, with hairpin curves on both sides of the pass. On the western ascent, a viewpoint has directional markers identifying Sierra Nevada peaks surrounding the lake. East of the crest, overlooks face Reno and Washoe Valley. The Nevada Department of Transportation designated approximately 20 miles of Route 431 as the Mount Rose Nevada Scenic Byway in 1996.

The road existed by 1950 as access to Mount Rose’s ski areas. Then it was dirt, passable by automobile only during summer. Before 1976, the highway carried the number State Route 27. The ski country itself changed as well: the Reno Ski Bowl opened in 1953, and the separate Mount Rose Ski Area opened in 1964 before the two operations merged in 1987.

Begin at Route 28 in Incline Village on Lake Tahoe’s northeast shore and climb to Mount Rose Summit. The highway’s highest point is the 8,911-foot pass between Slide Mountain and Tamarack Peak. Descending east, pass the ski area and the valley overlooks before the bends lead into Galena, part of Reno. The highway ends at US 395 Alternate and Route 341.

moments.title: Incline Village
moments.text: Incline Village takes its name from a railway built to lift timber out of the Tahoe basin. The Sierra Nevada Wood and Lumber Company operated here during the late-1800s mining boom, when the Comstock Lode needed wood. Logs traveled 1,400 feet up the incline before entering a gravity flume. The settlement was established in 1882, and its post office opened in 1884. Incline Creek shares the railway’s name and flows through the village to Lake Tahoe. The lumber also supplied home and commercial construction in Virginia City and Carson City, beyond the needs of the mines.

moments.title: Mount Rose Summit
moments.text: Mount Rose Summit is a pass, with Slide Mountain on one side of the saddle and Tamarack Peak on the other. At 8,911 feet, it is the highest point reached by Highway 431. A parking area and small building serve the highway stop. The highway takes its name from Mount Rose, which stands off the road. The bends on both approaches mark the crossing of the Carson Range. On the western climb, the marked viewpoint identifies peaks surrounding Lake Tahoe; on the eastern side, the overlooks face Reno and Washoe Valley.

moments.title: Mount Rose Ski Tahoe
moments.text: The ski area’s name can mislead: its slopes are on Slide Mountain, across Highway 431 from Mount Rose. The Reno Ski Bowl opened on Slide Mountain’s east face in 1953 and hosted the first NCAA Skiing Championships the next year. Chosen as a backup venue for the 1960 Olympic downhill, it gained a competition course and facilities that the Games never needed. A plaque in the lodge commemorates that Olympic role. The separate Slide Mountain and Mount Rose ski areas merged in 1987. The 1954 collegiate championship was hosted by the University of Nevada.
